paragraphs: This paper asks whether the way images are converted into tokens changes how effectively generation can be improved through search. In test-time search, a system explores candidate outputs and uses a verifier to judge them. Conventional image tokens describe locations on a grid, whereas ordered tokens can describe an image progressively, moving from broad structure toward finer details.

The proposed explanation is that coarse-to-fine sequences produce meaningful intermediate images. A verifier can assess these partial results and guide subsequent choices before generation finishes. Controlled experiments support this hypothesis: autoregressive models using ordered tokens benefit more from additional search than their grid-based counterparts.

The authors also demonstrate text-to-image generation by searching ordered token sequences without training an autoregressive model, using an image-text verifier for guidance. This training-free result concerns the autoregressive generation component. The study further examines best-of-N, beam search, and lookahead search alongside different verifiers and autoregressive priors. Together, the findings show that token structure influences both what a model learns and how effectively search can steer its outputs.
icml-2026-1d-ordered-tokens-enable-effic.tldr: Coarse-to-fine image tokens make intermediate generations easier to evaluate, improving search-guided generation in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: ArcDAE addresses a tension in learning representations that support both image reconstruction and semantic tasks. A representation needs enough detail to recreate an image, but it should also expose meaningful features. The paper argues that separating these functions loses information, while tightly coupling them through unrestricted reconstruction can force random, high-frequency detail into the compressed representation.

The method modifies the diffusion bridge that connects representation learning with generation. Its constraint changes with the diffusion timestep and separates semantic directions from the space associated with stochastic noise. This encourages the bottleneck to retain features useful for discrimination while discarding redundant high-frequency information. Generation and semantic representation remain coupled, without requiring the bottleneck to carry every noisy detail.

Experiments with ArcDAE trained on FFHQ report improvements over state-of-the-art methods of up to 6.4% in downstream semantic regression and 9.7% in reconstruction fidelity. These are reported maximum gains, rather than uniform improvements across every evaluation. The findings support the paper’s central idea that controlling what enters the shared representation can improve semantic usefulness and reconstruction together.
icml-2026-arcdae-asymmetric-rectified-co.tldr: ArcDAE filters stochastic detail from a shared diffusion representation to improve both semantic prediction and image reconstruction.

paragraphs: Interactive world models generate video as a user takes actions. When they rely on recent frames without an explicit three-dimensional environment, they must learn geometric consistency implicitly, and their spatial memory is limited by the available temporal context. This makes maintaining a coherent environment over extended interaction difficult.

PERSIST instead models an evolving latent 3D scene, including the environment, camera, and renderer. New frames are synthesized from this persistent state. The approach gives the model a continuing spatial representation to work with as the experience changes, connecting visual generation to an underlying scene rather than only to a history of pixels.

Quantitative evaluation and a user study report substantial improvements in spatial memory, geometric consistency, and stability over long interactions compared with existing methods. The authors also demonstrate generating diverse 3D environments from one image and controlling experiences through direct editing and specification in 3D space. These capabilities show how persistent scene state can support both visual continuity and more precise, geometry-aware user control.
icml-2026-beyond-pixel-histories-world-m.tldr: PERSIST maintains an evolving 3D scene to improve spatial memory, geometric consistency, and control in interactive video generation.

paragraphs: This paper questions whether improving test loss is enough to establish desirable generalization in diffusion models. It identifies a training phase in which test loss keeps decreasing while generated samples become unusually close to training examples. A model can therefore improve under a standard evaluation criterion while becoming more dependent on the particular data it saw.

To measure this bias, the authors train the same network on two disjoint datasets and compare distances among generated samples and their proximity to training data. They demonstrate the phenomenon on real images. They then investigate its emergence with a controlled hierarchical data model that provides exact scores and known underlying statistics.

The proposed mechanism is sequential feature learning. Broad structure is learned early in a relatively data-independent way, while later learning of finer features increasingly reflects individual training samples. This makes the timing of training relevant beyond the test-loss curve alone. The results suggest that stopping at minimum test loss may be insufficient for privacy-critical applications, even when that stopping point is optimal under conventional generalization criteria.
icml-2026-biased-generalization-in-diffu.tldr: Diffusion models can improve test loss while generating samples increasingly close to training data, complicating privacy-sensitive early stopping.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to estimate treatment effects for different kinds of individuals when randomized experiments are expensive but historical observations are plentiful. Historical targeting policies can leave some groups heavily treated and others rarely treated. Such imbalance and missing overlap make observational data alone unreliable for estimating what treatment changes.

The proposed framework uses those observations to choose which individuals should enter additional randomized experiments. Selection considers uncertainty about treatment uplift, differences between data domains, and gaps in treatment overlap. Repeating this process directs a limited experimental budget toward samples expected to be especially informative for causal estimation.

The authors provide finite-sample error bounds, asymptotic normality results, and lower bounds establishing near-optimality in a linear representation setting. Synthetic experiments support the theory. Extensions to industrial scenarios using neural uplift models show that active selection can use randomized samples more efficiently than random selection. The theoretical near-optimality applies to the stated linear setting, while the broader neural applications receive empirical support.
icml-2026-budgeted-active-experimentatio.tldr: The framework uses observational data to target limited randomized experiments where they can most improve treatment-effect estimation.

paragraphs: Conditional generation can produce several plausible outputs for the same input, so evaluating one output may miss important variability. This paper introduces a reliability score that considers the worst performance within a prediction set constructed at a chosen confidence level. The score connects evaluation to uncertainty by examining a set of possible outputs rather than a single generated result.

Computing that score is difficult because generated outputs can be high-dimensional, and both the evaluation function and the prediction set can have complicated, nonconvex shapes. The proposed CReL framework addresses both parts of the problem: building a set with the desired coverage and optimizing the reliability score within it.

The authors establish theoretical coverage results and report more informative prediction sets than existing approaches. Experiments on synthetic data, image-to-text generation, and text-to-image generation support the metric’s interpretability and the framework’s computational effectiveness. The worst-case assessment is specifically over the constructed prediction set at the selected confidence level; it does not claim to cover every conceivable output.
icml-2026-conformal-reliability-a-new-ev.tldr: CReL evaluates conditional generation through worst-case performance within a prediction set calibrated to a chosen confidence level.

paragraphs: Category-level 6D pose estimation learns to recover object position and orientation across object categories. The paper identifies a problem with fully shared models: categories with very different geometry can push shared parameters in incompatible directions. These conflicting training updates can cause negative transfer, where learning across categories harms performance.

DecomPose begins with gradient-based diagnostics that locate this conflict within model modules. It then groups categories using a data-derived measure of difficulty and routes examples through separate correspondence branches. This separates incompatible updates. Its capacity allocation is deliberately asymmetric: structurally simpler categories receive larger branches to act as stable training anchors, while complex categories receive lightweight branches to limit noisy updates.

Experiments on REAL275, CAMERA25, and HouseCat6D report reduced conflict between categories and improved pose estimation across the benchmarks. The contribution connects an observed training problem to a targeted architectural change. In particular, the results support assigning branch capacity according to optimization stability, rather than assuming that geometrically more complex categories should always receive more capacity.
icml-2026-decompose-disentangling-cross-.tldr: DecomPose separates conflicting category updates and allocates branch capacity by training stability to improve object pose estimation.

paragraphs: Preference alignment trains language models using judgments about which responses people prefer. Real preference datasets can contain sensitive prompts and judgments, creating privacy concerns during post-training. DPPrefSyn addresses this by learning from private preferences and producing synthetic preference data that can support subsequent alignment.

The framework first fits a preference model with formal differential privacy guarantees, then combines that learned model with public prompts to generate synthetic comparisons. Its design uses the Bradley–Terry model for pairwise preferences and the geometric structure of the data. Cluster-specific reward models share a linear structure, allowing the method to represent heterogeneous preferences while exploiting common information. Differentially private principal component analysis improves learning accuracy.

Experiments show competitive alignment performance under strong differential privacy guarantees. The findings support synthetic preferences as a practical route to privacy-preserving alignment: the private learning stage captures preference patterns, and public prompts provide inputs for synthesis. The paper’s central contribution is a structured method for producing useful preference data while formally protecting the private data used to learn those patterns.
icml-2026-differentially-private-prefere.tldr: DPPrefSyn learns a differentially private preference model and uses public prompts to synthesize data for competitive language-model alignment.

paragraphs: A unified multimodal model may answer questions and generate images using internal knowledge, but updating its textual answers does not necessarily update its pictures. This paper studies that transfer problem with UniKE, a benchmark containing 2,971 edit subjects covering changes to attributes and relations. Generated images are checked through visual question answering.

The evaluations reveal a large gap between modalities. Text-side editing efficacy can reach approximately 92%, while the best overall visual-question-answering accuracy for direct image generation is 18.5%. These measurements show why successful textual editing alone is an unreliable indicator that generated images will reflect the same update.

The authors propose Reasoning-augmented Parameter Editing, which explicitly activates the edited knowledge before image generation. It improves visual accuracy for every evaluated model-editor pairing, with gains up to 18.6 percentage points. Mechanistic analysis associates the gap with incomplete alignment between edited text representations and the pathways conditioning visual generation. The results motivate editing methods that account for how each modality accesses and uses updated knowledge.
icml-2026-do-text-edits-generalize-to-vi.tldr: UniKE reveals that successful text knowledge edits often transfer poorly to image generation, while explicitly activating edits improves visual results.

paragraphs: Understanding a video requires tracking both what a scene contains and how actions change it. The paper argues that multimodal language models struggle to organize these changes systematically across videos or image sequences. DynaVieW addresses this by making scene states and transitions explicit parts of a learned world model.

Training uses alternating sequences of states and transitions. States describe broad scenes drawn from video keyframes, while transitions organize dynamic elements within a hierarchical schema. A mixture-of-experts architecture jointly learns to predict transitions and simulate resulting states. Selective attention across experts and a loss that reweights schema tokens support learning of these structured descriptions.

This organization links an account of what happens to an account of what the visual world becomes afterward. The reported gains extend to visual narrative creation and world simulation, including more consistent and controllable generation and improved instruction following. The findings support structured modeling of visual change as a useful way to improve downstream generation, rather than treating temporal understanding as an implicit by-product of processing image sequences.
icml-2026-dynaview-schema-guided-world-m.tldr: DynaVieW learns structured sequences of scene states and transitions to improve visual prediction, simulation, and controllable generation.

paragraphs: Malicious behavior can be spread across several source files, with dependencies that become hard to follow amid large amounts of harmless code. This paper tackles that localization problem by organizing a project as a graph before asking a language model to perform detailed security analysis. The graph provides a way to retain relationships across code sections.

The pipeline uses a language model to encode graph nodes with semantic and structural information, then trains a graph neural network with sparse supervision. The graph network makes an initial detection. Interpreting its predictions identifies influential regions that are likely to contain malicious behavior, and those regions guide the language model’s subsequent analysis.

This division of work reduces interference from irrelevant context while keeping annotation costs low. Experiments on multiple public and custom datasets report consistent improvements over existing approaches. The findings support graph-based localization as a useful first stage for language-model code analysis, especially when understanding suspicious behavior requires connecting evidence across files. The reported results indicate practical potential for software security deployment.
icml-2026-efficient-code-analysis-via-gr.tldr: A graph neural network identifies suspicious code regions and directs a language model toward cross-file malicious behavior.

paragraphs: Translation evaluation is more useful when it explains why one translation is preferable to another. FiRE addresses reference-free evaluation, where a reference translation is unavailable. Instead of asking for one overall judgment, it uses existing language models to compare translation pairs separately for faithfulness, fluency, and consistency of style.

Separating these criteria makes the judgment more interpretable: a comparison can identify which aspect of quality favors each candidate. To evaluate this approach, the authors construct a human-annotated benchmark for fine-grained, reference-free ranking. They report substantial agreement among annotators, providing support for using these judgments to assess automated evaluators.

On that benchmark and existing MQM datasets, FiRE aligns more closely with human comparative judgments than regression-based and error-analysis metrics. It also provides more detailed feedback about translation quality. The paper examines position bias, evaluators’ tendency to favor their own outputs, and handling of ties. These analyses help explain how language-model comparisons should be interpreted alongside the reported gains in agreement with human rankings.
icml-2026-fire-fine-grained-ranking-eval.tldr: FiRE compares translations by faithfulness, fluency, and style, producing rankings that better match human judgments in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Recruiting workers through social connections is complicated when tasks require physical attendance. Someone influenced to take interest may still be unable to participate. Tasks also have finite demand, so attracting more workers ceases to add value once that demand is met. These features make social reach alone an inadequate recruitment objective.

GKD-Recruiter targets effective task satisfaction by combining two kinds of information. A heterogeneous graph models worker-task compatibility, while a directional graph attention mechanism models social influence. Graph knowledge distillation combines these signals. The framework then uses Rainbow DQN to search recruitment choices in a setting where demand saturation creates difficulties for greedy selection.

Experiments on a real-world dataset report better solution quality and faster inference than state-of-the-art baselines. The results support considering actual task fulfillment throughout recruitment, including compatibility and saturation. The approach matters because recruitment choices interact: the value of reaching another worker depends on which tasks still need people, as well as whether that worker is socially reachable and able to execute the task.
icml-2026-gkd-recruiter-jointly-modeling.tldr: GKD-Recruiter combines worker-task compatibility and social influence to improve recruitment under physical participation constraints and finite task demand.

paragraphs: Quantized observations retain discretized measurements rather than full continuous values. Recovering statistical information from them becomes harder when the underlying distribution departs from assumptions used by existing methods. This paper develops inference within the normal variance-mean mixture family, which includes Gaussian, t, and several generalized hyperbolic distributions.

The main computational obstacle is a likelihood involving difficult multidimensional integrals from both quantization and hidden mixture variables. The proposed expectation conditional maximization algorithm introduces latent variables for both sources of complexity. It uses the family’s conditional Gaussian structure to obtain closed-form parameter updates at each iteration, making the optimization procedure tractable.

The authors establish global linear convergence guarantees for the proposed algorithm and extend the framework beyond basic parameter estimation. Applications include quantized regression, matrix completion, compressive sensing, and covariance estimation. Numerical experiments report effectiveness and robustness across quantized inference problems. The contribution is a common computational framework that supports a broader collection of distributions and structured recovery tasks while retaining convenient iterative updates.
icml-2026-inference-from-quantized-data-.tldr: A latent-variable algorithm makes inference from quantized observations tractable across a broad family of statistical distributions.

paragraphs: Protein interaction predictors often invest in powerful representations of individual proteins but combine them using generic classification operations. This paper focuses on the final interaction decision. It draws on the biological L3 rule, under which multiple paths of length three between two proteins indicate a greater likelihood that they interact.

The authors first provide empirical evidence that widely used interaction datasets support this rule. Their L3-PPI module then generates a prompt graph from protein representations, adding virtual length-three paths and controlling their number through regularization. The prediction becomes a classification of this generated graph, allowing its structure to express an interaction prior based on complementarity.

Because the module operates on protein representations, it can be attached to leading predictors without requiring a completely new representation-learning system. Extensive experiments report stronger performance enhancements than state-of-the-art competitors. The findings support improving the classification head itself with biological structure: how two protein representations are combined can be an important source of predictive improvement alongside the quality of those representations.
icml-2026-learning-the-interaction-prior.tldr: L3-PPI improves protein interaction prediction by turning protein pairs into graphs that encode a biologically motivated length-three-path prior.

paragraphs: Learned fluid simulators can accelerate physics computation, but this paper argues that their training procedures often neglect important numerical structure. Supervising individual mesh nodes and using simple explicit time updates can overlook local spatial relationships and stiff dynamics. The authors address these training choices across several model architectures.

The framework introduces three changes. Multi Node Prediction predicts values over a node’s local neighborhood to enforce consistency in spatial derivatives. Temporal Correction uses cross-attention in a predictor–corrector scheme to improve time evolution. Three-dimensional rotary positional embeddings provide geometric information intended to capture rotational symmetries on unstructured meshes.

Evaluation covers MeshGraphNet, Transolver, and a Transformer on diverse physics datasets. The framework consistently improves accuracy and stability, particularly when predictions are repeatedly fed forward over long rollouts. Its latent representations also generalize to unseen subtasks, including wall shear stress and pressure prediction. These results support incorporating numerical and geometric structure into training objectives and time updates, alongside continued development of simulation architectures.
icml-2026-mesh-based-simulations-with-sp.tldr: Spatially coordinated predictions, temporal correction, and geometric embeddings improve the accuracy and long-rollout stability of learned mesh simulators.

paragraphs: Object detectors that combine modalities must decide both how to fuse features and where to connect their processing streams. The paper argues that matching features only at corresponding backbone stages is insufficient because the modalities can remain substantially different at those stages. Useful complementary information may require connections across stages.

MFH-NAS searches local fusion operations and the larger pattern of connections together. Differentiable search learns parameters for local fusion choices, while evolutionary search explores stage selection and cross-stage topology. Combining the two is intended to balance refinement of promising choices with exploration, reducing premature convergence to a limited fusion design.

Evaluations on LLVIP, RGBT-Tiny, and M3FD show consistent improvements over handcrafted fusion-stage designs and earlier stage-searching methods. The abstract reports an increase in mAP@0.5 from 85.3% to 88.2% over strong fixed-stage fusion methods, alongside gains across all three benchmarks. The findings support searching fusion connectivity and fusion operators jointly, allowing the architecture to discover complementary information beyond predefined stage alignment.
icml-2026-mfh-nas-a-hybrid-neural-archit.tldr: MFH-NAS jointly searches fusion operations and cross-stage connections to improve multimodal object detection.

paragraphs: Neural flows model irregularly sampled time series by directly learning trajectories that would otherwise require numerical differential-equation solvers. This provides efficiency, but many approaches underuse relationships among variables. Learning those relationships is particularly challenging when a single mapping replaces the repeated interaction refinement available in step-by-step methods.

Graph-Structured Neural Flows add two forms of auxiliary trajectory supervision. Re-initializing trajectories makes their divergence reveal graph-driven interactions, with a theoretical lower bound characterizing that divergence. Generating trajectories backward in time adds a consistency requirement between forward and reverse evolution. The latter uses flow invertibility to help regularize the learned graph.

These auxiliary tasks give interaction learning additional structure while preserving the one-step flow approach. On five real-world datasets, GSNF achieves state-of-the-art classification performance with highly competitive training time and memory usage. The reported results suggest that direct trajectory models can capture useful variable relationships when their training includes explicit signals about how interactions affect trajectory changes and reversibility.
icml-2026-one-step-graph-structured-neur.tldr: GSNF uses auxiliary forward and reverse trajectories to strengthen interaction learning in efficient one-step time-series models.

paragraphs: Structure learning seeks to recover relationships among variables from data. Conditional independence testing asks whether two variables remain dependent after accounting for other variables. This paper establishes a formal connection between the best achievable statistical rates for these tasks, turning a relationship between problems into a tool for analyzing their difficulty.

The authors construct a general reduction for poly-forests, the graph setting covered by their result. Within these problems, the minimax rate for conditional independence testing determines the minimax rate for structure learning. Minimax rates describe performance in the hardest cases within the specified model class, so the result concerns fundamental statistical requirements rather than only the behavior of one implementation.

The framework yields optimal rates for Bernoulli, Gaussian, and nonparametric examples. A suitable modification of the PC algorithm achieves optimality in these settings. The contribution provides a unified route to analyzing structure learning through testing complexity, with concrete optimal algorithms for the studied cases. Its stated scope is the poly-forest reduction and associated examples.
icml-2026-optimal-structure-learning-and.tldr: For the studied poly-forest settings, optimal conditional independence testing rates determine optimal structure-learning rates.

paragraphs: Service agents must manage a conversation while making decisions that affect both user experience and operational cost. Empathetic communication and budget constraints can pull behavior in different directions. InteractCS-RL treats task-oriented dialogue as a reinforcement learning problem with feedback at multiple levels, allowing training to address these strategic trade-offs.

The framework supplies an interaction environment with persona-driven users so agents can explore diverse strategies. Its Cost-aware Multi-turn Policy Optimization combines a hybrid advantage estimator with credit for the generative process. A PID-Lagrangian controller adjusts how cost constraints influence learning, guiding exploration of the trade-off boundary between user reward and global cost.

Experiments in customized real business scenarios report significant improvements over baselines across three evaluation dimensions. Additional tool-agent-user benchmarks support robustness across different domains. The findings suggest that training agents around complete interactions and explicit cost control can improve their ability to balance service utility with resource limits. The goal is to learn favorable trade-offs between competing objectives, rather than maximize user reward without accounting for expense.
icml-2026-reinforcing-real-world-service.tldr: InteractCS-RL trains service agents to balance user rewards and operational costs through multi-turn reinforcement learning and adaptive cost control.

paragraphs: Molecules vary in both atom count and spatial extent. Diffusion architectures can accept different numbers of atoms, but the paper identifies a separate issue: molecular size changes how coordinate scale compares with noise. Consequently, handling variable input size alone does not make the generative process consistent across molecules.

The authors analyze generation as an initial formation of coarse structure followed by refinement of atomic positions. Larger molecules develop coarse structure earlier because their spatial scale is greater relative to the noise. Decomposing denoising dynamics shows how this scale difference affects both three-dimensional structure and atom types, making molecular size influence the progression of generation.

Scaling the Prior adjusts the prior distribution according to molecular size. The aim is to normalize learning and bring denoising trajectories into better alignment across sizes while generating high-quality molecules. This approach changes the starting distribution to address a mismatch in the generative process itself. The central insight is that variable-sized geometric data require attention to spatial scale as well as the number of modeled elements.
icml-2026-scaling-the-prior-size-consist.tldr: Scaling the Prior adjusts diffusion’s starting distribution by molecular size to align generation across different spatial scales.

paragraphs: This paper redesigns attention to help language models operate on sequences much longer than those used in training. It separates attention into two stages: forming normalized weights and sharpening their distribution. The motivation is that conventional Softmax attention can encounter numerical instability and degraded performance as inference length increases.

The first stage replaces Softmax with Softplus followed by l1 normalization and adds a dynamic scale based on invariance entropy. The second reweights attention to strengthen significant weights and reduce weaker ones. This sharpening helps concentrate attention on relevant tokens and mitigates the attention sink phenomenon. The authors report improvements over conventional attention and leading Softmax-free alternatives.

In the reported evaluations, validation loss remains nearly constant at sixteen times the training length, with stronger long-context retrieval and downstream results. Symbolic regression experiments also recover Newton’s gravitational law from orbital trajectories. That result provides evidence for the authors’ argument that attention design matters for learning physical structure, alongside the more direct evidence for numerical stability and length extrapolation.
icml-2026-softplus-attention-with-re-wei.tldr: Softplus normalization and attention sharpening improve numerical stability and maintain nearly constant validation loss at sixteen times training length in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Protein-engineering models are increasingly expected to prioritize future experiments, which differs from predicting measurements scattered randomly across an existing dataset. TadA-Bench evaluates this prospective ranking problem using a million variants from 31 rounds of TadA directed evolution. It preserves the experimental chronology so earlier rounds provide data for ranking variants appearing only later.

The benchmark is a fixed-data replay of a wet-lab campaign. It offers aligned DNA, RNA, and protein views, while Seq2Graph reconciles noisy enrichment measurements into activity labels that can be compared across rounds. This design makes the historical sequence of discovery part of the evaluation rather than mixing past and future observations.

Random-split controls show strong interpolation, but ranking future-round variants and selecting candidates under finite budgets prove much harder. Controlled analyses suggest that coverage of evolutionary variation is more informative than local data density. The benchmark therefore exposes a gap between fitting available measurements and prioritizing later experimental candidates, providing a reproducible setting for studying the latter capability.
icml-2026-tada-bench-a-million-variant-b.tldr: TadA-Bench preserves experimental chronology to reveal how much harder future protein-variant discovery is than random-split prediction.

paragraphs: Steering modifies a language model’s internal representations to influence its behavior, but similar interventions can produce different outcomes across inputs. This paper argues that theories assuming independently controllable, orthogonal concepts cannot adequately explain that variability. Its Cylindrical Representation Hypothesis retains linear concept representations while allowing their contributions to overlap.

The resulting geometry is specific to each sample. A central axis describes the main semantic transition, while a perpendicular plane governs sensitivity to steering. Within that plane, some sectors encourage activation of the target concept and others suppress or delay it. The theory distinguishes what can be inferred from difference vectors: they reveal the plane, but not its sensitive sectors.

Experiments across 100 concepts, multiple models, and different steering methods consistently support the predicted cylindrical structure. This offers an explanation for why well-aligned intervention directions can still behave inconsistently. The evidence suggests that some variability comes from representation geometry itself, and that identifying a good direction may leave uncertainty about how an individual sample responds.
icml-2026-the-cylindrical-representation.tldr: The Cylindrical Representation Hypothesis explains steering variability through overlapping concept geometry and sample-specific regions of sensitivity.

paragraphs: This paper makes language-model circuits easier to understand by training transformers with most weights fixed at zero. Each neuron consequently has only a small number of connections. The goal is to build models whose internal computations are more readable, making it easier to identify mechanisms underlying particular behaviors.

For several handcrafted tasks, the authors prune the trained models further to isolate the responsible circuits. These often contain neurons and residual channels associated with recognizable concepts, connected through a small number of interpretable relationships. The paper reports rigorous validation of these circuits and a high degree of human understandability.

The scaling study finds a trade-off: greater sparsity improves interpretability at a cost to capability, while larger models improve the balance between the two. Preserving interpretability beyond tens of millions of nonzero parameters remains challenging. Preliminary results also suggest the method could be adapted to explain existing dense models. Thus, the strongest evidence concerns models trained for sparsity, while application to already-trained dense systems remains exploratory.
icml-2026-weight-sparse-transformers-hav.tldr: Training transformers with sparse weights produces unusually readable task circuits, with a measured trade-off between interpretability and capability.
